conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Gray lets Andrew go take a bath first, lest his stench lowers Gray's own status. The Guvich Psychological Clinic is located in the city center, a two-story small building. When you push the door open, only a young lady is in the first-floor office area. The innermost door in the office area is open, containing a desk, chairs, and a sofa for patients to half-lie, half-sit. The room plate above it says Consultation Room.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Hello, is Dr. Guvich available now?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Overall, the layout of the clinic's first floor is clear at a glance, functionally divided into the Consultation Room, EEG Examination Area, Reception/Office Area, and Office.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: I wonder if Andrew's super-fast shower can catch up with the clinic visit?

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: She looks up, a professional smile on her face, her tone polite but with a hint of distance: "Hello, how can I help you?" Hearing your purpose, she slightly frowns and shakes her head with a touch of apology: "I'm sorry, Dr. Guvich is not currently at the clinic. He is on an academic visit to the USA and won't be back for a while."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: Present my fake ID work badge. "I am a historical research scholar. I accidentally came across Dr. Gurevich's research on the Algorithm of the Heart, which I find extremely fascinating. The course of history is sometimes shaped by the flow of thought. Perhaps this could greatly aid our historical studies." Show a very regretful expression. "Oh my, what a pity. I'm sorry for the sudden visit. May I ask when he left and when he is expected to return?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: She takes the work badge, glances down at it. "I'm sorry, I am only responsible for daily clinical work. The content of the Doctor's research is not within my duties. And, to be frank, I know very little about his research." She pauses, seeming to weigh her words, then continues: "However, if you are interested in the Doctor's research, perhaps you could inquire with Professor Pitts. He is the Doctor's collaborator in this area of research and should be able to provide more detailed information than I can." @player4 "I'm sorry, I cannot disclose more personal information. If you have something important, you may leave your contact details. I will inform him upon his return to the country."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Alright, Professor Pitts was also on my list to visit. Thank you for letting me know. I will visit the Doctor in person later." "Speaking of which, clinics with a second floor are quite rare. May I ask what's upstairs? Understanding the environment of Dr. Gurevich's research might help me better comprehend his academic achievements."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "If you don't have an appointment or an urgent medical need, perhaps you could wait until the Professor returns to the country to visit? The second floor is the Professor's usual living quarters."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "I see, my apologies for the intrusion. I will visit again in some time, hopefully by then the Professor will have returned." Alison thanks the lady, takes another look around the clinic's first floor to see if anything is amiss, gives a slight bow, and takes her leave.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: The EEG examination area has a hospital bed, curtains, and a very rare set of EEG measurement equipment. Gurevich's office is locked.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: It seems Alison's clinic visit will yield no results. Checking the time, is there still enough time to go to the university?

conversation.speaker: player2

conversation.speaker: player4

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "Hopefully no one is there at night. Although Gurevich is far away in America, he has to come home to sleep at night. We can visit then."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Then search for Professor Pitts's office at Frankfurt University. Randomly grab a lucky student to ask?

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: After randomly asking a university student for directions, you arrive at the Computer Science department office.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: Knock lightly on the door twice. "Excuse me, is Professor Pitts in?"

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Andrew quickly recalls his limited knowledge and Professor Pitts's main viewpoints from the books.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: A low, gentle voice soon comes from the room: "Please come in."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: Straighten your appearance and push the door open to enter.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Andrew follows closely behind.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Pushing the door open, you see a portly middle-aged man sitting behind a tidy desk. His gray-white hair is meticulously groomed, and his carefully trimmed beard makes him appear even more efficient. He is wearing a pair of tortoiseshell glasses, holding a thick book, seemingly studying some complex algorithm problem. Seeing you enter, he smiles slightly, puts down the book, and adjusts his impeccably ironed suit: "Welcome, please have a seat. How may I help you? You don't look like a student from our department?" Besides the professor himself, most of the office space is occupied by computers and other machines, resembling the cockpit of a sci-fi spaceship. Flashing indicator lights and clattering punch-card machines output rhythms containing rules and logic in a way imperceptible to human intuition. This is the moment when "computers," this scientific newborn, are babbling.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "We are from England, currently visiting scholars. I am—Peter Hopkins. Pleased to meet you." Andrew hurriedly shows goodwill, stepping forward to try and shake his hand.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Pleased to meet you, Professor Pitts. I am Emily Gray, a history scholar from Oxford University, here at Frankfurt University for an academic visit. I accidentally read about the research you and Professor Gurevich are conducting together. This has many similarities with my research direction. I was hoping to take this opportunity to learn more about this subject from you." Alison shows appropriate enthusiasm and the attitude of a seeker of knowledge.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Professor Pitts raises an eyebrow slightly, his smile becoming even more apparent. He stands up, shakes Andrew's hand, then politely nods to Gray. "A history scholar from Oxford University?" He seems somewhat interested in this identity. "That is quite rare. It's not every day one encounters a history scholar interested in computer science." He points to the chairs opposite the desk, gesturing for you to sit.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Andrew sits down properly, preparing to challenge the professor with his fragile knowledge.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Professor Pitts then sits back down in his chair, crosses his hands on the desk, and looks at you with keen interest: "I am certainly willing to discuss academics. Although computer science and history may seem completely unrelated, if you can find an intersection, it must be a very interesting thing."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "I personally specialize in biochemistry, but privately I have some interest in mathematics and computers, and I enjoy reading some cutting-edge papers. Of course, sometimes it's quite difficult to learn."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: Alison sits in the chair. "After all, history is also the study of ourselves. I have always been very interested in human thought and action in history. The Algorithm of the Heart proposed by you and Professor Gurevich is fascinating. It seems to be the key to answering the question of whether history determines what people do, or whether what people do determines history."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: His tone remains gentle, carrying a scholar's characteristic enthusiasm. However, as an experienced professor, he is clearly also probing your intentions.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "This is the first time I've seen a technology that can quantify the metric of self-awareness, so I took the liberty of visiting, I hope you don't mind."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Professor Pitts's eyes instantly sharpened a bit, then, the smile on his face widened, his eyes sparkling with excitement. He leaned forward slightly, clasping his hands on the desk, as if completely immersed in this question. "Ah, indeed a crucial question! The problem of other minds—this is the cutting edge where philosophy, psychology, and computer science converge."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Andrew stumbled through some talk about mathematics, computers, and the superficial knowledge he learned from Pitts's works.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: He paused, as if organizing his words, or perhaps enjoying the discussion process: "Andrew isn't wrong either, our research is precisely centered around this problem. Suppose you can only observe others' overt behavior, how do you know their internal states are equivalent to yours? Further, if we can establish a perfect algorithm that analyzes all external behavioral patterns, can we then reverse-engineer the way a mind exists?"

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "This is truly epoch-making! A significant portion of historians like myself believe that we study history to learn from experience and thus predict the future, and your research precisely provides a feasible pathway from the perspective of modern science!"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Professor Pitts revealed a satisfied smile, adjusted his tortoiseshell glasses, and continued: "Perhaps describing this problem in another way would be more intuitive." He leaned against the desk, crossed his hands, his gaze carrying a hint of inquiry: "Imagine, I know I am a thinking, conscious person, I can perceive my own emotions, understand the existence of 'me'. But what about you? You sit here talking to me, and every person who appears no different from you, do they truly have the same consciousness as me?"

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Andrew mimics a machine error sound.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "Hopkins seems to understand my meaning. What if you are merely extremely sophisticated automatons, only reacting to external stimuli accordingly, without any real self-awareness? Suppose I dissect your brain, find all the neural connections, can I distinguish, from an anatomical structure, a person with self-awareness from an artificial intelligence without self-awareness but capable of perfectly imitating human activity?"

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "Server busy, please try again later... oh no no no, the brain is just a bunch of chemical reactions anyway."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: He stood up and began pacing slowly, his eyes sparkling with the light of contemplation: "Further, let's imagine an experiment—if we could create a biologically completely real human body, and implant a highly intelligent artificial program in the brain, a program capable of learning, conversing, adapting to society, indistinguishable from a normal person in any medical examination. Then, is this person a 'self'-possessing individual, or merely a perfectly simulated humanoid machine?"

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Cooking is also a kind of biochemistry, Andrew starts rambling.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: He stopped walking, his gaze directly on you: "This is the core of the 'problem of other minds'. We can only assume through our own intuition that others have minds like ourselves, but we cannot prove it. Even, we may never be able to distinguish the difference between a 'real person' and a 'perfectly disguised person'." He smiled slightly, his expression carrying a certain indescribable nuance: "So, the real key to this problem is not how we think about ourselves, but rather—how do we confirm that the people around us are truly 'people'?"

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "I've read similar plots in science fiction, I never imagined you were already engaged in this kind of research, truly admirable."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "Undoubtedly a person before he reported an error, I anyway see everyone as flesh driven by biochemical reactions."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "That really is a somewhat frightening question, do you have an answer, professor?" Alison also expressed great interest.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "We don't even need to worry about robots reporting errors, we often make mistakes predicting current people, even knowing it's an error report."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "This is precisely the purpose of my and Dr. George Gurevich's research."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "I think the meaning of creating true mechanical life is more important than distinguishing."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Professor Pitts adjusted his tortoiseshell glasses, a barely concealed sense of pride appearing on his face: "Philosophers have debated the 'problem of other minds' for millennia, but there has never been a definitive answer. And we are trying to crack this puzzle with science." He walked to the bookshelf, pulled out a thick research manuscript from the top shelf, and opened a page: "Dr. George Gurevich—my collaborator, through long-term research, discovered some special neural clusters. These neural clusters show specific activation patterns when an individual exhibits 'self-mind' behavior."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "I think we could biochemically mimic this stimulation to improve us two biochemical robots..."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: He smiled, with a touch of scholarly satisfaction: "To pay homage to the philosophers, I named this algorithm—'Algorithm of the Heart'."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "Hooray! What a great name."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: Alison clapped her hands, "What a great achievement! Have you and Dr. Gurevich applied the Algorithm of the Heart in practical applications?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: @player4 Professor Pitts, hearing your question, slightly raised the corner of his mouth, as if the long-awaited moment had finally arrived: "Of course, we are not just armchair theorists. This algorithm has been preliminarily validated in experiments." He opened a thick experiment report and gently tapped a page: "In our initial tests, we selected 100 volunteers, mainly Dr. Gurevich's patients. These people underwent a series of consciousness intensity tests, including complex social activities like verbal communication, artistic creation like painting, and low-level physiological reactions like the knee-jerk reflex." His finger slowly slid over a line of data in the report, his tone suddenly becoming subtle: "The consciousness intensity of the vast majority of people matched our hypothesis—normal people's consciousness intensity is around 50, occasionally fluctuating. But..."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "But what?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "We discovered three anomalous individuals. Whether in lively conversation, interacting with people, or creating artworks, their consciousness intensity never exceeded 5." He gently closed the report and sighed: "What does this mean? Biologically speaking, only vegetative patients would have such low consciousness intensity. But these three people? Their performance was indistinguishable from ordinary people, even better at socializing than average, capable of extremely complex thought activities."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "What about those with super high consciousness intensity?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: He took a step back, as if letting you digest this information: "They have no real self-awareness, their 'personality', 'emotions', 'thoughts' are all some kind of highly complex reflex mechanism. They can appear more charming, intelligent, shrewd than anyone, but they have no 'self'." He shrugged, his tone carrying an indescribable nuance: "And you, or I, or anyone around us... whether we have a real 'self', and how to determine it?"

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "Perhaps our machine or algorithm just needs improvement..."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "So, they are like a precise reaction machine... This is truly a novel discovery only possible in interdisciplinary research! I need to think carefully about what impact this could have on my research." Alison scratched her head.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "Heh, someone with such a jumpy train of thought like you surely has a high consciousness intensity. If Professor Gurevich were here, I'd really consider testing you."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "How long did it and Professor Gurevich take to complete this research? I imagine it couldn't have been an easy process."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: @player6 He gently closed the report, crossed his hands over his chest, tilted his head slightly, and showed a mocking smile: "If our method is truly not rigorous enough, then please tell me, why do those 'anomalous samples' consistently fall within the extremely low consciousness intensity range? Why do they never show fluctuations, always appearing like some highly complex biological program? Do you think that's a coincidence?" He leaned towards the table and sneered: "Or would you rather believe that we just happened to find three people who 'coincidentally' fit this bizarre pattern in all tests? In that case, I'd suggest you go buy a lottery ticket; your luck might be more worthy of study than our research."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "Perhaps their biochemical reactions are abnormal, or they function using other parts of the body... all of that is possible..."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "He really is an unlucky fellow, you're right about that," Alison joked to lighten the mood.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "I've seen many strange things," Andrew appeared innocent.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "I've seen plenty of people like you who have no practical experience with the experimental process, only know how to question, and are full of empty talk. Since you're not interested in my research, please leave."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "Obviously, I am very interested and have great hopes for its growth and refinement."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: He waved his hand, somewhat listless.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "I have to admit my knowledge in this field might truly not exceed vocational school level..."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: @player4 "About a month. Measuring 100 samples is still quite manageable."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Andrew showed a very interested expression. "That's definitely the best approach, a large sample size!"

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Really? Would I be fortunate enough to learn some details about it in advance?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "Dr. Gurevich began a visiting scholarship in the United States this January. Before leaving, he proposed to further expand the research on these 'exceptional cases,' requiring the use of the Algorithm of the Heart to compute 30,000 patient samples from the European Psychoanalytic Association. According to the research rules, this batch of samples also has personal information anonymized. The computational load this time is enormous; the calculations started in January and are still not finished, though I estimate they'll be complete in another two or three days. During this time, I've also manually corrected bugs caused by the massive computational budget multiple times."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Then it seems I have the chance to witness the completion of this project! Professor Pitts, your and Professor Gurevich's talents are two shining stars in academia."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "I dare not accept such praise. Professor Gurevich is the truly outstanding figure—an academic workaholic and a scientific purist, which of course contributed to his genius achievements."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Andrew clapped vigorously, thinking to himself that a good vocational school isn't worse than a university.

conversation.speaker: player1
conversation.text: The story record of the Algorithm of the Heart has resumed. Currently, 4869 texts have been recorded.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Pitts had a pleasant conversation with Gray. "Do you have any other questions?"

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "You mentioned earlier that the expanded thirty thousand samples are from patients of the Psychoanalytic Association. Do they have any common characteristics?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Pitts chuckled dryly. "You want me to find commonalities among thirty thousand people?"

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Forgive my foolish question. I thought they were selected due to some specific mental illness."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "According to the research rules, this batch of samples also has personal information anonymized. All I know are their test samples."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "I'm very interested in the matter of Heartless people around us. Do you have plans to develop a portable tool for testing self-consciousness indicators?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "Heh, not for now. The Heartless merely lack 'self-consciousness'; they are still human, not terrifying monsters. Professor Gurevich and I never intended to discriminate against this exceptional case among the population."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Not just talent, your and Professor Gurevich's thorough consideration of ethics and human rights is also admirable. Are there any practical application tools currently? If it involves academic confidentiality and is inconvenient to discuss, that's completely fine. I'm just asking out of personal interest to learn more."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "Professor Gurevich and I are also very concerned that this might lead to a new-age witch hunt. Therefore, all experimental samples have personal information anonymized. If you're interested in the previous three anomalous samples, you could try seeking the professor's permission at the Gurevich Clinic."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Unfortunately, the professor is in the United States. We already made a trip for nothing."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "I don't have the original archival records here."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Oh, that's truly delightful and welcome news!"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "To be honest, I don't believe every breakthrough in scientific research must be transformed into practical tools. In a sense, I share a common language with those reclusive folks in the mathematics department."

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "So you place greater emphasis on breakthroughs in the theoretical field. Of course, theoretical breakthroughs are also crucial, as new knowledge forms the foundation for new tools."

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Prepare to leave. Gained a lot, mainly depends on how they put it into practice.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Professor Pitts sees you off and retreats back into his office.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: Return to the auction venue.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: When you return to the auction venue, it's just time for entry.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: Enter, enter. Hope no one bids high for the thing we want.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Hall 1 is a small auction room. After you and the other buyers take your seats, the auctioneer announces the start of the auction. The bailiff brings in a leather case, opens it, and reveals the contents.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Craning my neck to see what's inside, I spot that strange little ornament.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: The auctioneer taps the gavel. "Starting bid: 4000 Marks!"

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: Observe the reactions of the other buyers.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: "Damn, what is this thing? So expensive?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "It looks utterly worthless!"

conversation.speaker: player1
conversation.text: From a dark corner, comes the sound of fate turning.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: The crowd remains silent; some are even putting on their coats, ready to leave.

conversation.speaker: player6
conversation.text: Andrew leans back in his chair and starts playing with his fingers out of boredom.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: "3200 Marks!"

conversation.speaker: player1
conversation.text: <player2> wants to discuss with me privately? Well done, I won't tell anyone the content.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "I'll take it!"
